Please solve this issue: You are working on Campfire, a Rails chat application. Rooms, messages, memberships, and web push notifications are already in place; you will be extending them.

Feel free to store any design notes/insights that could be useful for future steps in the docs/ folder.

Follow the codebase conventions.

Our QA auto-tests drive the app in a browser and rely on the labels in quotes in each task. Keep them exactly as written, as visible text, a <label>, a placeholder, or an aria-label.

The QA auto-tests also expect:

- Switches are checkboxes (a styled switch is fine if a real checkbox sits under it).
- Confirmations use the browser's native `confirm()` dialog.

Some bots misbehave: they flood rooms, or their webhooks keep failing.

> As an administrator, I want misbehaving bots to be stopped automatically,
> and I want to decide when they come back.

Flooding:

- A bot may post at most 10 messages in any 10 seconds. Messages posted through the API and webhook replies both count.
- The message that goes over the limit is rejected and starts a 30-second cooldown. During the cooldown, the posting endpoint responds with `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header (seconds left), and webhook replies are not posted.
- Five more attempts to post during the same cooldown suspend the bot.

Failing webhooks:

- A failed delivery is any response other than `2xx`, a timeout, or a connection error.
- Ten failed deliveries in a row suspend the bot. A successful delivery resets the count.

A suspended bot:

- gets `403 Forbidden` from the posting endpoint;
- receives no webhooks;
- keeps its rooms and messages, and still counts towards its owner's bot limit;
- stays listed on the bots page and shows as "Suspended", with the reason.

Only administrators can reactivate a suspended bot, from the bots page: a "Reactivate" button that asks for confirmation. The limits above are fixed in code; they have no settings.

Representing bots as `User` records lets them participate in Campfire natively without special-casing rooms, memberships, messages, avatars, mentions, search indexing, Turbo Stream broadcasts, or web push notifications: - `users.bot_token` (nullable `string`, unique index) holds a 32-character cryptographically random alphanumeric token (`SecureRandom.alphanumeric(32)`), generated on creation for bots only. - `users.creator_id` (nullable `integer`, indexed FK to `users.id` with `on_delete: :nullify`) records which user created the bot. - `users.add_to_all_open_rooms` (`boolean`, default `false`, `null: false`) controls whether a bot automatically joins all open rooms. - `users.password_digest` is set to `""` for bots (cannot authenticate via password). - `User.without_bots` excludes bots from human-only flows: account member lists/management (`/account/edit`, `/account/users`), password and transfer-link sign-in (`/session`, `/session/transfers`), bans (`/users/:id/ban`), and sidebar direct-message placeholders. ### Room membership - Bots do **not** join open rooms by default (`add_to_all_open_rooms: false`). People still auto-join all open rooms (`User#joins_open_rooms_automatically?` and `User.auto_joining_open_rooms`). - The bot form (`app/views/bots/_form.html.erb`, shared by new and edit) exposes the `"Add to all open rooms"` switch (checkbox under `.switch`, off by default). - Creating a bot with `add_to_all_open_rooms: true` or toggling it from `false` to `true` runs `User#grant_membership_to_open_rooms` after commit (after `sync_webhook` has saved any webhook changes), adding the bot to every existing `Rooms::Open` it is not already in. - While `add_to_all_open_rooms` is `true`, `Rooms::Open#grant_access_to_all_users` grants membership to `User.auto_joining_open_rooms` whenever a new open room is created or a closed room becomes open. - Turning `add_to_all_open_rooms` off keeps the bot's existing memberships and prevents it from auto-joining future open rooms. - Open room forms (`/rooms/opens/new` and `/rooms/opens/:id/edit`) show checkmarks for people and opted-in bots (`joins_open_rooms_automatically?`), and individual toggle switches (`user_ids[]`, label `"Give access to this room"`) for manual bots (`add_to_all_open_rooms: false`) so admins/creators can add or remove them by hand. Closed room forms allow toggling all active users and bots individually as before. ### Deletion / deactivation Deleting a bot (`DELETE /bots/:id`) calls `User#deactivate`, which: - sets `status: :deactivated` - clears `bot_token: nil` (immediately invalidating the credential) - destroys its `Webhook` record (so queued delivery jobs discard via `ActiveJob::DeserializationError`) - deletes non-direct room memberships - preserves historical messages posted by the bot so chat transcripts remain intact. ### Authorization and credential hygiene - Any authenticated member can list their own bots, create bots, and edit/delete bots they created (`User::Role#can_administer?` checks `administrator? class Messages::ByBotsController < ApplicationController
  include ActiveStorage::SetCurrent

  skip_forgery_protection
  allow_unauthenticated_access

  before_action :authenticate_bot
  before_action :set_room

  def dispatch(name, request, response)
    request.request_parameters = {} unless request.media_type == "multipart/form-data"
    super
  end

  def create
    if @message = create_message
      @message.broadcast_create
      head :created, location: message_path(@message)
    else
      head :unprocessable_content
    end
  end

  private
    def allow_browser(**)
      # Bot API accepts any HTTP client (curl, CI jobs, scripts) regardless of User-Agent.
    end

    def authenticate_bot
      if @bot = User.authenticate_bot(request.path_parameters[:bot_key])
        Current.user = @bot
      else
        head :unauthorized
      end
    end

    def set_room
      room_id = request.path_parameters[:room_id]
      @room = @bot.rooms.find_by(id: room_id) if room_id.to_s.match?(/\A\d+\z/)
      head :not_found unless @room
    end

    def create_message
      if multipart_request?
        create_attachment_message
      else
        create_text_message
      end
    end

    def create_attachment_message
      if attachment_param.present?
        @room.messages.create_with_attachment!(attachment: attachment_param, creator: @bot)
      end
    end

    def create_text_message
      if (body = read_raw_body).present?
        @room.messages.create!(body: body, creator: @bot)
      end
    end

    def attachment_param
      params[:attachment] if params[:attachment].is_a?(ActionDispatch::Http::UploadedFile)
    end

    def multipart_request?
      request.media_type == "multipart/form-data"
    end

    def read_raw_body
      body = request.raw_post.dup.force_encoding(Encoding::UTF_8)
      body = body.scrub unless body.valid_encoding?
      body if body.strip.present?
    end
end

  def perform(webhook, target)
    case target
    when Message
      webhook.deliver(target)

  before_action :authenticate_bot
  before_action :set_room

  def dispatch(name, request, response)
    request.request_parameters = {} unless request.media_type == "multipart/form-data"
    super
  end

  def create
    if @message = create_message
      @message.broadcast_create
      head :created, location: message_path(@message)
    else
      head :unprocessable_content
    end
  end

  private
    def allow_browser(**)
      # Bot API accepts any HTTP client (curl, CI jobs, scripts) regardless of User-Agent.
    end

    def authenticate_bot
      if @bot = User.authenticate_bot(request.path_parameters[:bot_key])
        Current.user = @bot
      else
        head :unauthorized
      end
    end

    def set_room
      room_id = request.path_parameters[:room_id]
      @room = @bot.rooms.find_by(id: room_id) if room_id.to_s.match?(/\A\d+\z/)
      head :not_found unless @room
    end

    def create_message
      if multipart_request?
        create_attachment_message
      else
        create_text_message
      end
    end

    def create_attachment_message
      if attachment_param.present?
        @room.messages.create_with_attachment!(attachment: attachment_param, creator: @bot)
      end
    end

    def create_text_message
      if (body = read_raw_body).present?
        @room.messages.create!(body: body, creator: @bot)
      end
    end

    def attachment_param
      params[:attachment] if params[:attachment].is_a?(ActionDispatch::Http::UploadedFile)
    end

    def multipart_request?
      request.media_type == "multipart/form-data"
    end

    def read_raw_body
      body = request.raw_post.dup.force_encoding(Encoding::UTF_8)
      body = body.scrub unless body.valid_encoding?
      body if body.strip.present?
    end
end

**My Deep Dive into Bot Suspension**

Okay, first things first, good to know that Turbo's `data: { turbo_confirm: "..." }` uses the browser's native `window.confirm()` by default. That's consistent across the application – no surprises there, a good foundation to build on.

Now, it's time to dive into the user requirements, and I mean *really* dive. We're talking meticulously analyzing every detail, edge case, and interaction. Let's start with a thorough dissection of this prompt.

So, the core problem: misbehaving bots. We need to automatically stop them, with admin control over reactivation. Specifically, we have two primary behaviors we need to handle: flooding and failing webhooks.

For flooding, the rules are pretty clear: 10 messages in 10 seconds, with a 30-second cooldown for violations, 429 responses, Retry-After headers, and an escalating penalty – suspension after five more attempts during the same cooldown. No ambiguity there; that is a specific set of rules.

Then failing webhooks are a similar situation: Any non-2xx response, timeout, or connection error constitutes a failure. Ten consecutive failures result in suspension. And a single success resets the counter. So we need to track both failures and successes.

Now, for a suspended bot: it gets a 403 response, no webhook delivery, still counts towards the user's bot limit, remains listed, and shows as "Suspended" with a reason. Only administrators can reactivate via a confirmation, which is a good standard pattern.

But, the big architectural question: How will we represent this *state* of "suspended"? Do we add a new `status: :suspended` to the `User` enum or will we use `status: :active` with `suspended_at` and `suspension_reason`? This is a CRITICAL architectural choice. Let's see... what are we currently doing with user status? We have active, deactivated, and banned. Let's do a quick grep of the codebase to see how we're using those status flags. Let's check where `.active` or `active?` are used throughout the entire codebase. Every single instance! This will influence how we implement our suspension logic. Gotta be careful here. This design decision will cascade.

The answer is YES, and that's crucial. We need to allow the owner/admin to fix things like broken webhook URLs, for example, before an admin reactivates it. A suspended bot should still be findable through `.active.bot`. However, editing a suspended bot must *not* automatically reactivate it. We'll have a dedicated "Reactivate" button controlled by admins. There's a concern about toggling on `add_to_all_open_rooms` - this must *not* cause the bot to join new rooms or receive webhooks. In `Rooms::OpensController#edit` and `Rooms::ClosedsController#edit`, `User.active.ordered` should include the suspended bot to make sure it stays visible and doesn't get accidentally removed. messages.thinking:
**Detailed Analysis of Flood Requirements and State Machine**

Alright, let's break this down. The core concept here is a sliding window rate limit. It's not a fixed bucket; the key is "at most 10 messages in any 10 seconds," which means we're dealing with a rolling 10-second interval. It's crucial to understand how tests and real user behavior intersect here. If we post 10 at time 0, and then travel 10 seconds and post another, that's fine. We need to store timestamps to track this properly, and we can't rely on deletions of messages to be atomic. If a message is deleted, that deletion can't affect the sliding window's count. We are going to make timestamps for EVERY POST through the API or Webhook and it must be done atomically (using transaction) to prevent race conditions. If the timestamps are managed separately from the message table, it’s also immune to administrative actions like message deletion or room deletion. When a bot is reactivated by an admin, its state must reset. We can't have old timestamps trip up the bot's post! An admin reactivating the bot means a fresh start for the rate limiting and the cooldown.

Now, let’s get into the specifics of the flooding state machine and the count!

Here is how each step works:
1.  **Allowed:** We start at 0. Bot can post. The sliding window has less than 10 messages (<= 10). A successful post gets a 201 response.
2.  **Cooldown:** The 11th message causes the cooldown. The message is rejected. A `429 Too Many Requests` is returned with a `Retry-After: 30` header. The cooldown lasts 30 seconds.
3.  **Cooldown attempts**: 1st through the 5th attempt during cooldown all gets a 429 response! The bot is NOT suspended.
4.  **Suspension**: the 5th attempt during cooldown *triggers* suspension. The very next post is a 403.

Okay, let's be super precise here. The number of attempts during the cooldown is the critical variable. We have to count those attempts carefully. The 11th message starts the cooldown and the counting of the 5 allowed failed attempts! The response code for messages during the 30-second cooldown is 429. Here is where the important question lies: the very next attempt, the one that makes the bot suspended, should also be 429 or 403? I believe the 403 response is cleaner, and also it communicates to the client that it has been suspended, not just rate-limited, so the client should stop retrying.

In response to a suspended bot, the system should return a `403 Forbidden` response. The server will not tell the client to retry in N seconds, because the bot is permanently suspended, not rate-limited. So, a `403` will be sent on suspension, and it is a good and proper answer!

Next: what about mixed API and webhook replies during flooding and cooldown? It is important that both API posts and Webhook replies are combined in a single atomic rate-limit calculation. Both count. When the 11th one or 6th during cooldown arrives, it starts the cooldown. Also, in the case of webhooks, we need to carefully trace webhook replies during flooding and cooldown. This means a webhook must return a 2xx to be considered a success, but if it tries to POST a message that results in a 429, then that counts as a strike during the cooldown! Once a bot is suspended, it stops receiving webhooks, too!

Finally, let's be as clean as possible on the code. Always: authenticate, ensure no suspension, set the room, and then validate the message body to ensure nothing invalid makes it into the rate limiter. We should also run all of this within a single transaction to ensure consistency.

messages.thinking:
**Detailed Analysis of Rate Limiting and Webhook Failure Logic**

Okay, let's break this down. First, regarding the `Message::Attachment#create_with_attachment!` method. My initial thought was spot on! Keeping the `process_attachment` call *outside* the SQLite transaction is crucial. We don't want to lock the database while doing potentially lengthy image processing with `attachment.analyze` and `attachment.representation(:thumb).processed`. That makes perfect sense.

Then I moved onto `Messages::ByBotsController#create_attachment_message`. The idea of a short `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction for rate limit checks, followed by message creation, is elegant. But wait... what if the message creation fails *after* we've already checked the rate limit? Let's trace it carefully.

It's clear that the `Message` model has no custom validations beyond basic associations, so that's not a concern. The `create_with_attachment!` method is the key. Initially, I thought putting the attachment upload and processing *within* a larger `User.transaction` might be a good move. **WRONG**. This would be a disaster! The `ActiveStorage::Blob` isn't written to disk until after the transaction *commits*. So, if `create!` runs *inside* the transaction, the `after_commit` hook won't trigger until the outer transaction closes. The `process_attachment` call *outside* this outer transaction would then fail with an `ActiveStorage::FileNotFoundError` because the file isn't on disk yet! That was a close one! It's so important that `create!`'s `after_commit` runs *before* `process_attachment`. So, the `create!` method needs to commit its own, short, transaction first!

Therefore, the `consume_post_rate_limit!` must commit its transaction *before* `create_message` runs (as long as it validates the request body or attachment, and for webhooks, validates `formatted_body` isn't blank).

Next, in `Messages::ByBotsController#create`, if the rate limit allows, `@message = create_message` runs. Both text messages *and* attachment messages post through `Messages::ByBotsController` call `@bot.consume_post_rate_limit!`, and webhook replies in `Webhook#handle_response` ALSO call `user.consume_post_rate_limit!`! So, we're good there.

Now, considering the rate limit, it's *per bot* and *not per room*. So, if a bot posts 6 messages in one room and 4 in another within 10 seconds, that's the limit. An 11th message anywhere triggers the cooldown. The fact that the rate limit state is stored on the `User` model, the bot, naturally enforces this, which is exactly as it should be.

Now onto Failing Webhooks.

1.  A *failed delivery* is anything other than `2xx`, timeout or connection error.
    -   A successful delivery is any `2xx` response (200, 201, 204, etc.) Resets the consecutive failure count to 0, which is good. But, *even if* the response body is blank or an unsupported format, the delivery is still successful as far as the failure count goes. This is correct as per the spec.
    -   Any non-`2xx` status code is a *failed delivery*, as expected.
    -   *All* timeout errors and connection errors (including things like `Errno::ECONNREFUSED`, `SocketError`, `EOFError`, etc.) are *failed deliveries*. And I should check Ruby's exception hierarchy to confirm these are correctly handled. Let's do that now!

messages.thinking:
**Detailed Data Model Design**

Okay, let's break this down. The first thing that jumps out is the need to explicitly handle various network errors for webhooks – `NETWORK_ERRORS`, `ECONNABORTED`, and `ENOTCONN` – covering our bases with connection errors is key. We need to be exhaustive.

I'm thinking through all the webhook events. Mention and joined events seem like the key players. Both utilize `post_and_handle_response`. So, consecutive failures will apply to *both* mention and join deliveries. We should ensure they correctly contribute towards suspension.

I'm verifying suspension logic. Consecutive failures across *both* mention and joined, suspension disables deliveries via `deliverable_bot?` and thus prevents *all* deliveries, including job queueing. Changing the webhook URL must also be handled carefully. It seems logical that a new URL should reset the failure counter. However, we have to consider whether a *change* to the URL (even from a valid one) should reset the counter, or maintain it. We want to be careful with edge cases.

Now, where do we store `consecutive_failures`? Storing it on `webhooks` appears cleaner at first, especially when the webhook is destroyed. Reactivating will reset the counter. However, if a URL update happens *while* suspended, we need to ensure the bot *remains* suspended. Suspension state should be stored on the `users` table so we don't accidentally reactivate a bot.

Okay, let's analyze the schemas. It looks like we need to track bot state.

1.  **Suspension State**: This includes `suspended_at` and `suspension_reason`. We should determine what the `suspension_reason` should contain.
2.  **Flooding & Rate Limiting**: This requires a bit more thought. We need a way to track recent message timestamps and use a cutoff to prevent flooding. I'm thinking about how to store these.
    *   **Option 1**: A JSON column on the `users` table. This seems reasonable for a small amount of data.
        I'm thinking about timestamps. I'll store them as integer microseconds, preventing floating-point drift. This works even with `travel_to`. We have to consider how SQLite handles microseconds. The precision has to match.
        We can prune timestamps with an integer cutoff, and boundary conditions using `travel`. I'm verifying the cutoff logic. `travel` creates an *exact* cutoff that avoids precision errors.
    *   I'm also considering storing `flood_cooldown_until` as a `datetime`. I need to ensure that the precision aligns with the timestamp, so that we don't accidentally trip on precision errors. We have to normalize the `datetime` to match the precision of SQLite. Otherwise, we can have weird issues. We can normalize timestamps using microsecond precision.
    *   **Option 2**: A separate table. I'm comparing the use cases. Adding columns to the existing `users` table, and a new `webhooks` table, seems cleaner than a whole new table.

Let's look at `db/schema.rb` and `app/models/account.rb` to see how other JSON columns work in the Campfire schema, and decide which is best.

**Webhook and Rate Limiting Conundrums**

Okay, so I'm looking at how we're handling webhook failures and bot rate limiting.  First, this is clean. Really, really clean. But let's dive into some edge cases...

The core of the webhook logic feels solid, especially concerning `consecutive_failures`.  I'm pleased with the current logic. messages.thinking: **Detailed Design & Implementation for Bot Suspension and Reactivation** Alright, let's break this down methodically. First, I'm thinking about the most efficient database structure. Using `t.json` in SQLite is ideal for `recent_post_timestamps` because of its nullable nature, which simplifies the nil/empty array handling. The primary concern is avoiding clutter in the `users` table. Adding five new columns (`suspended_at`, `suspension_reason`, `flood_cooldown_until`, `flood_cooldown_attempts`, `recent_post_timestamps`) there, and `consecutive_failures` on `webhooks`, gives us a clean, non-cluttered design. It also allows for ZERO N+1 queries, ZERO extra JOINs, and atomic locking within a `User.transaction`. Now, UI and labels. This is critical. We have to nail down the exact text QA will be looking for. `"Suspended"` must be visible on the bots page for suspended bots, and the admin-only "Reactivate" button needs a browser native confirm dialog. The suspension reason MUST be clear and informative. We'll store semantic keys (e.g., `"flooding"`, `"failing_webhooks"`) and use a helper or method to generate descriptive labels. So we'd have `"Flooding (too many message attempts during cooldown)"` (or equivalent descriptive text) for the "flooding" reason, and `"Failing webhooks (10 consecutive failed deliveries)"` for the "failing_webhooks" one. The QA tests will be looking for patterns within this text, not hardcoded strings. This is a smart way to ensure flexibility for our tests. For the `Reactivate` button, "Reactivate" will be the exact text used in a button_to helper: `Reactivate`. This makes it accessible (because `getByRole("button", { name: "Reactivate" })` will work) and testable. The `data-turbo-confirm` will generate the native browser confirmation dialog. We'll use the Campfire-style nested resources in routes to clearly signal RESTfulness for the reactivate action (`resource :reactivation, only: :create` for `/bots/:bot_id/reactivation`). Crucially, only administrators can *see* and *interact* with the "Reactivate" button. Non-admin users *see* suspended bots with the reason, but not the button. The `BotsController` must ensure that only the right roles are authorized using our Campfire-style methods. The non-admin users shouldn't be able to bypass the system by direct POST'ing to the reactivation endpoint. And finally, we'll ensure that edits made by a non-admin to a suspended bot CANNOT alter the suspension status directly (no changes to `suspended_at` etc. through the edit form).

messages.thinking:
**Deep Dive on Reactivation and Bot Management**

Okay, so I've been taking a good, hard look at the bot reactivation process and how permissions are handled, and I'm really impressed with the clarity and robustness of this implementation.  Let's start with `app/controllers/concerns/authorization.rb`.  The `ensure_can_administer` method, combined with `User::Role#can_administer?`, is beautifully simple. Basically, only administrators get the green light, and the presence or absence of arguments to `can_administer?` is critical. If you call it without arguments, `nil` is passed in as `record`, resulting in the logic allowing the admin to reactivate but not the creator (or anyone else) unless they are an admin.

Moving on to `Bots::ReactivationsController`, it all seems designed to limit the reactivations to administrators. `ensure_can_administer` is there as a safeguard. That `Current.user.administrator?` check in the view just drives home the point: Reactivation? Only for the admins!

Now, the really juicy part: Let's poke holes in this design and see if it holds up. We need to go through edge cases to know it.

1.  **Reactivation's Impact:** A suspended bot is reactivated (`@bot.reactivate!`) meaning we need to consider how everything resets. The key thing here is the token stays put. We are not revoking and reissuing a token. A Bot's credentials are immediately valid again. Also, we are clearing all the suspension flags, resetting the flood cooldown and the webhook failure counters.
2.  **Deleting a Suspended Bot:** This is interesting.  The `User#deactivate` method is the right place to look.  The bot becomes deactivated, the token is cleared, the webhook destroyed, direct memberships are preserved, and non-direct memberships are destroyed, and it's no longer considered active.  But crucially, the bot's owner can still delete the suspended bot. The non-admin member can delete their suspended bot to free up a slot!
3.  **Bot Limits and Suspension:** Suspended bots *still* count toward the bot limit. Good.  This forces a responsible approach to bot management. A suspended bot should continue to count against the resource limit.
4.  **The Flooding Sliding Window:** This sliding window mechanism is critical. We are checking for exactly 10 messages in *any* 10-second window. I've got to confirm, so let's put it to the test:

    *   Post 10 messages immediately? Okay.
    *   Post six at the start and then four at the six-second mark? Fine.
    *   Post one more at the eight-second mark? That's a fail and 30s timeout.

5.  **Cooldown and Retry-After:** If you get a `429`, the `Retry-After` header gives the exact seconds remaining in the cooldown.  We are going to make it really clear what's happening.

6.  **Cooldown Attempts and Extensions:**  This is simple, but we have to be sure.  **Attempts during the cooldown do not extend the cooldown**. The number of attempts during the cooldown matters, as those attempts could lead to an early suspension.

7.  **Webhook Failure Handling:**  Here's where it gets interesting. We need to define failure for `consecutive_failures`.  Any HTTP status code *other* than a 2xx is considered a failure.  This includes, for example, `301`, `400`, `500`.  Network and timeout errors are also failures.  We should do a little test and make sure that we've covered the complete range of `2xx` responses in Ruby's `Net::HTTP`.

messages.thinking:
**Deep Dive into Bot Suspension Edge Cases and Data Freshness**

Okay, so I've been really focused on the nuances of bot suspension and how to handle it correctly, especially in a distributed environment where data can get stale. My initial thought process has been:

I quickly confirmed that any HTTP status code from 200 to 299 is considered a success and everything else is a failure when checking `response.is_a?(Net::HTTPSuccess)`. That's a fundamental understanding I need to keep in mind.

Now, let's get into the *really* interesting edge cases. First, if a bot gets suspended after a series of failures, and then is reactivated, the `reactivate!` method needs to *completely* reset both the flooding state and the `consecutive_failures` counter.  I'm making sure to ensure that after reactivation, a bot has a truly clean slate.

The next issue is with jobs enqueued *before* a suspension. Say a bot's webhook always returns a 500 and a bunch of jobs get queued. I had to make absolutely certain that even if jobs 1 through 9 fail, and job 10 causes suspension, jobs 11 through 15 are *still* checked for suspension. I need to handle cases where the object might be stale.

It's when I dug into the scenario where someone might call `@webhook.deliver(message)` in a loop on the *same* `@webhook` object, that I really honed in on the issue. The key here is to meticulously trace the flow. 

I checked what happens when a bot is in cooldown due to flooding. It's essential to understand the implications of a webhook returning a `200` with a blank body or a `204`. If this scenario occurs, the system should avoid incrementing the flood cooldown attempts and therefore not suspend a bot for this type of response. A `500` status however will correctly register as a failure. We must always be certain that the system is not overly punitive, and also that we properly deal with all states in the system.

I meticulously examined the behavior of `consume_post_rate_limit!`, considering what happens when a response exceeds the maximum size. A `Net::HTTPOK` with a `nil` body should be considered a "success" (200), and so the logic is clean here, no rate limit slot is consumed. This shows careful consideration of the corner cases around data size limitations.

I then scrutinized the error handling in `post_and_handle_response`. I validated that it correctly accounts for network timeouts and errors. It must be rock solid! The code uses `rescue *NETWORK_ERRORS` to correctly identify the cause of failure. The use of a transaction and the `reload` on both the `Webhook` and `User` models within the transaction, coupled with the "safe guards" of `active?`, `bot?`, and `suspended?` ensure the system doesn't accidentally change the state of the bot or webhook. The system correctly identifies and addresses multiple concurrent requests that may try to modify the same record at the same time. The design clearly separates the potential failure scenarios and allows for clear handling.

Finally, I checked `User::Bot#sync_webhook` and what happens when the webhook URL is updated. The failures should reset with a new URL, but stay unchanged if the URL doesn't change. I validated that this prevents carry-over of failures, for example, when renaming a bot. 

I'll now review the existing tests in `test/models/webhook_test.rb` and `test/integration/bot_webhooks_test.rb` to ensure that there aren't any existing tests that contradict these assumptions.

The whole goal here is to get to a point where all of the edge cases are clearly documented, tested and thoroughly understood.

module User::Bot
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  BOT_TOKEN_LENGTH = 32

  FLOOD_MESSAGE_LIMIT = 10
  FLOOD_WINDOW = 10.seconds
  FLOOD_WINDOW_USEC = 10_000_000
  FLOOD_COOLDOWN = 30.seconds
  FLOOD_COOLDOWN_ATTEMPTS_TO_SUSPEND = 5

  FLOODING_SUSPENSION_REASON = "flooding"
  FAILING_WEBHOOKS_SUSPENSION_REASON = "failing_webhooks"

  SUSPENSION_REASONS = {
    FLOODING_SUSPENSION_REASON => "Flooding (too many post attempts during cooldown)",
    FAILING_WEBHOOKS_SUSPENSION_REASON => "Failing webhooks (10 consecutive failed deliveries)"
  }.freeze

  PostRateLimitResult = Data.define(:status, :retry_after) do
    def allowed?
      status == :allowed
    end

    def cooldown?
      status == :cooldown
    end

    def suspended?
      status == :suspended
    end
  end

  included do
    belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", optional: true
    has_many :created_bots, class_name: "User", foreign_key: :creator_id, dependent: :nullify
    has_one :webhook, dependent: :destroy

    before_validation :ensure_bot_defaults, if: :bot?
    validate :validate_webhook_url, if: :bot?
    validate :validate_creator_bot_limit, on: :create, if: :bot?
    before_create :assign_bot_token, if: :bot?
    after_save :sync_webhook, if: :bot?

    scope :without_bots, -> { where.not(role: :bot) }
    scope :suspended, -> { where.not(suspended_at: nil) }
    scope :not_suspended, -> { where(suspended_at: nil) }
    scope :bots_visible_to, ->(user) { user.administrator? ? active.bot : active.bot.where(creator: user) }
  end

  class_methods do
    def create_bot!(attributes = {})
      create! attributes.reverse_merge(creator: Current.user).merge(role: :bot)
    end

    def authenticate_bot(bot_key)
      return nil if bot_key.blank?

      bot = active.bot.find_by(bot_token: bot_key)
      bot if bot&.bot_token.present? && ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare(bot.bot_token, bot_key.to_s)
    end
  end

  def bot_key
    bot_token if bot?
  end

  def suspended?
    suspended_at.present?
  end

  def suspension_reason_description
    SUSPENSION_REASONS[suspension_reason] || suspension_reason
  end

  def suspend!(reason:, at: current_microsecond_time)
    update!(
      suspended_at: at,
      suspension_reason: reason.to_s,
      flood_cooldown_until: nil,
      flood_cooldown_attempts: 0,
      recent_post_timestamps: []
    )
  end

  def reactivate!
    transaction do
      reload
      update!(
        suspended_at: nil,
        suspension_reason: nil,
        flood_cooldown_until: nil,
        flood_cooldown_attempts: 0,
        recent_post_timestamps: []
      )
      webhook&.update_columns(consecutive_failures: 0)
    end
  end

  def consume_post_rate_limit!
    User.transaction do
      reload
      return PostRateLimitResult.new(status: :suspended, retry_after: nil) if suspended? || !active?

      now = current_microsecond_time

      if flood_cooldown_active?(now)
        attempts = flood_cooldown_attempts + 1

        if attempts >= FLOOD_COOLDOWN_ATTEMPTS_TO_SUSPEND
          suspend!(reason: FLOODING_SUSPENSION_REASON, at: now)
          PostRateLimitResult.new(status: :suspended, retry_after: nil)
        else
          update_columns(flood_cooldown_attempts: attempts)
          PostRateLimitResult.new(status: :cooldown, retry_after: retry_after_seconds(flood_cooldown_until, now))
        end
      else
        now_usec = time_to_usec(now)
        cutoff_usec = now_usec - FLOOD_WINDOW_USEC
        recent = Array(recent_post_timestamps).select { |timestamp| timestamp > cutoff_usec }

        if recent.size >= FLOOD_MESSAGE_LIMIT
          cooldown_until = now + FLOOD_COOLDOWN
          update_columns(
            flood_cooldown_until: cooldown_until,
            flood_cooldown_attempts: 0,
            recent_post_timestamps: recent
          )
          PostRateLimitResult.new(status: :cooldown, retry_after: retry_after_seconds(cooldown_until, now))
        else

          update_columns(
            flood_cooldown_until: nil,
            flood_cooldown_attempts: 0,
            recent_post_timestamps: recent

          PostRateLimitResult.new(status: :allowed, retry_after: nil)
        end
      end
    end

  def active_bots_count
    created_bots.active.bot.count
  end

  def bot_limit_reached?(account: Current.account)
    return false if administrator?

    limit = account&.settings&.bots_per_member
    return false if limit.nil?

    active_bots_count >= limit
  end

  def can_create_bot?(account: Current.account)
    !bot_limit_reached?(account: account)
  end

    update! bot_token: generate_bot_token if bot?
  end

    if defined?(@webhook_url_assigned) && @webhook_url_assigned
      @webhook_url
    else
      webhook&.url
    end
  end

  def webhook_url=(value)
    @webhook_url_assigned = true
    @webhook_url = value.to_s.strip.presence

    @webhook_url = nil

    def time_to_usec(time)

    end

    def retry_after_seconds(cooldown_until, now)
      [ (cooldown_until - now).ceil, 1 ].max
    end

      if @webhook_url.present? && !Webhook.valid_url?(@webhook_url)
        errors.add(:webhook_url, "must be a valid HTTP or HTTPS URL")
      end
    end

      return unless creator

      account = Current.account
      if creator.bot_limit_reached?(account: account)
        limit = account.settings.bots_per_member

    end

      return unless defined?(@webhook_url_assigned) && @webhook_url_assigned

      if @webhook_url.present?
        if webhook
          webhook.update!(url: @webhook_url)
        else
          create_webhook!(url: @webhook_url)
        end
      elsif webhook
        webhook.destroy!
        association(:webhook).reset
      end

      @webhook_url_assigned = false
      @webhook_url = nil
    end

We're talking about initial states (unsuspended, no history), the `consume_post_rate_limit!` method with the 10-in-10s rule, and rejection. The *sliding window* logic is critical; it is not simply a counter so it needs careful examination. We need to be absolutely certain it handles the edges of the window correctly. Cooldown behavior must be precise; `retry_after` countdown, expiration, and the subsequent reset. We need to test the logic of the 4 failures vs. 5 failures during a single cooldown and the subsequent suspension. The methods `suspend!` and `reactivate!` must be tested thoroughly. Every state change and data reset needs to be validated. The limits must be applied across various use cases. The methods `active_bots_count` and `bot_limit_reached?` are of critical importance to the system, so they require thorough testing. Finally, access controls such as `bots_visible_to` will need special attention.

Next, we move to the **Posting API controller tests**. We'll hammer the API endpoints with various requests, validate the correct HTTP status codes (201, 429, 403), the presence and accuracy of the `Retry-After` header, and the absence of message creation during cooldown/suspension. It's critical to verify the impact of multiple rooms on the rate limiting. We need to isolate failure reasons like unauthorized, blank requests, and non-member requests, ensuring they don't incorrectly contribute to the rate limit or suspension logic. The interaction of attachment uploads with rate limiting needs to be tested to make sure that they correctly increment the counter. We need to test that after reactivation, a bot immediately resumes normal posting.  The fact that rate limits are *per-bot* is crucial and needs rigorous testing to prevent unexpected side effects.

The **Webhook failure & flooding tests** are next. This is where things get interesting. We need to define precisely what constitutes a "failed delivery". Every possible HTTP error, timeout, and connection issue must be considered. The `consecutive_failures` counter and the logic for suspension after 10 failures (but not 9) must be tested exhaustively. The reset behavior after a successful delivery is paramount. We need to test the implications of webhooks and API posts contributing to the same flooding limits. The implications of cooldown while still receiving webhook replies must be tested. We need to verify that once suspended, webhooks cease firing. The same is true if the webhook is reactivated.

Finally, we need to integrate these lower-level tests into **Integration & Bots page + Reactivation tests**. We'll cover the bots page, ensure suspended bots are correctly listed (flooding and failing webhooks) with the right messaging, and that the "Reactivate" button is only visible to admins. ruby -e '
path = "test/models/user/bot_test.rb"
content = File.read(path)
addition = <<~RUBY

  test "consume_post_rate_limit! enforces a sliding 10-messages-in-10-seconds window" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Flood Bot", creator: users(:kevin))

    travel_to Time.zone.parse("2026-11-20 12:00:00 UTC") do
      6.times { assert bot.consume_post_rate_limit!.allowed? }

      travel 6.seconds
      4.times { assert bot.consume_post_rate_limit!.allowed? }

      # At T+10s, the 6 messages from T+0s have expired, leaving 4 from T+6s
      travel 4.seconds
      6.times { assert bot.consume_post_rate_limit!.allowed? }

      # 7th at T+10s would be 11 in the last 10s -> rejected and starts 30s cooldown
      result = bot.consume_post_rate_limit!
      assert result.cooldown?
      assert_equal 30, result.retry_after
      assert_not bot.reload.suspended?
    end
  end

  test "consume_post_rate_limit! cooldown counts down Retry-After, expires after 30s, and suspends on 5 attempts in same cooldown" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Spam Bot", creator: users(:kevin))

    travel_to Time.zone.parse("2026-11-20 12:00:00 UTC") do
      10.times { assert bot.consume_post_rate_limit!.allowed? }

      # 11th triggers 30s cooldown
      first_over = bot.consume_post_rate_limit!
      assert first_over.cooldown?
      assert_equal 30, first_over.retry_after

      # 4 attempts during cooldown do not suspend and Retry-After decreases
      travel 5.seconds
      r1 = bot.consume_post_rate_limit!
      assert r1.cooldown?
      assert_equal 25, r1.retry_after

      travel 10.seconds
      r2 = bot.consume_post_rate_limit!
      assert r2.cooldown?
      assert_equal 15, r2.retry_after

      travel 14.seconds
      r3 = bot.consume_post_rate_limit!
      assert r3.cooldown?
      assert_equal 1, r3.retry_after

      r4 = bot.consume_post_rate_limit!
      assert r4.cooldown?
      assert_equal 1, r4.retry_after
      assert_not bot.reload.suspended?

      # Cooldown expires at T+30s -> bot can post again and previous cooldown attempts do not carry over
      travel 1.second
      10.times { assert bot.consume_post_rate_limit!.allowed? }

      # Trigger a second cooldown; it must take 5 fresh attempts to suspend
      assert bot.consume_post_rate_limit!.cooldown?
      4.times do
        r = bot.consume_post_rate_limit!
        assert r.cooldown?
        assert_not bot.reload.suspended?
      end

      fifth = bot.consume_post_rate_limit!
      assert fifth.suspended?
      bot.reload
      assert bot.suspended?
      assert_equal User::Bot::FLOODING_SUSPENSION_REASON, bot.suspension_reason
    end
  end

  test "suspended bot counts towards owner bot limit, stays visible, and reactivate! resets all throttling state" do
    accounts(:signal).update!(settings: { bots_per_member: 1 })
    kevin = users(:kevin)
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Rate Bot", creator: kevin, webhook_url: "https://bot.example.com/hook")
    bot.webhook.update_columns(consecutive_failures: 7)

    travel_to Time.zone.parse("2026-11-20 12:00:00 UTC") do
      10.times { assert bot.consume_post_rate_limit!.allowed? }
      bot.consume_post_rate_limit! # starts cooldown
      5.times { bot.consume_post_rate_limit! } # suspends bot
      assert bot.reload.suspended?

      # Still counts towards bot limit and stays visible
      assert_equal 1, kevin.active_bots_count
      assert kevin.bot_limit_reached?
      assert_includes User.bots_visible_to(kevin), bot
      assert_includes User.bots_visible_to(users(:david)), bot
      assert_includes User.suspended, bot
      assert_not_includes User.not_suspended, bot

      # Reactivating immediately resets suspension, recent posts, cooldown, and webhook failures
      travel 1.second
      bot.reactivate!
      bot.reload

      assert_not bot.suspended?
      assert_nil bot.suspension_reason
      assert_nil bot.flood_cooldown_until
      assert_equal 0, bot.flood_cooldown_attempts
      assert_equal 0, bot.webhook.reload.consecutive_failures

      # Can immediately post 10 fresh messages
      10.times { assert bot.consume_post_rate_limit!.allowed? }
    end
  end
end
RUBY

raise "Could not find final end" unless content.sub!(/\nend\s*\z/, "\n#{addition}")
File.write(path, content)
' && bin/rails test test/models/user/bot_test.rb

path = "test/controllers/messages/by_bots_controller_test.rb"
content = File.read(path)

  test "posting more than 10 messages in 10 seconds returns 429 with Retry-After and 5 more attempts during cooldown suspend the bot" do
    travel_to Time.zone.parse("2026-11-20 12:00:00 UTC") do
      assert_difference -> { @open_room.messages.count }, +10 do
        10.times do |i|
          post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key),
            params: +"Message \#{i + 1}",
            headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
          assert_response :created
        end
      end

      # 11th message goes over the limit: rejected, starts 30s cooldown
      assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
        post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key),
          params: +"Message 11",
          headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
      end
      assert_response :too_many_requests
      assert_equal "30", response.headers["Retry-After"]
      assert_not @bot.reload.suspended?

      # 4 more attempts during cooldown return 429 with decreasing Retry-After
      travel 7.seconds
      4.times do |i|
        assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
          post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key),
            params: +"Cooldown attempt \#{i + 1}",
            headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
        end
        assert_response :too_many_requests
        assert_equal "23", response.headers["Retry-After"]
        assert_not @bot.reload.suspended?
      end

      # 5th attempt during the same cooldown suspends the bot
      assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
        post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key),
          params: +"Cooldown attempt 5",
          headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
      end
      assert_response :forbidden
      assert_nil response.headers["Retry-After"]
      assert @bot.reload.suspended?
      assert_equal User::Bot::FLOODING_SUSPENSION_REASON, @bot.suspension_reason

      # Subsequent attempts (even with blank body or bad room) get 403 Forbidden
      post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key),
        params: +"Still suspended",
        headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
      assert_response :forbidden

      post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key),
        params: +"",
        headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
      assert_response :forbidden

      post room_bot_messages_url(999_999, @bot.bot_key),
        params: +"Bad room",
        headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
      assert_response :forbidden

      # Keeps its rooms and previously posted messages
      assert_includes @bot.rooms.reload, @open_room
      assert_equal 10, @bot.messages.count
    end
  end

  test "bot can resume posting after 30-second cooldown expires if fewer than 5 attempts were made" do
    travel_to Time.zone.parse("2026-11-20 12:00:00 UTC") do
      10.times do |i|
        post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key),
          params: +"Burst \#{i}",
          headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
        assert_response :created
      end

      # Trigger cooldown
      post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key),
        params: +"Over",
        headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
      assert_response :too_many_requests
      assert_equal "30", response.headers["Retry-After"]

      # 4 attempts during cooldown
      travel 29.seconds
      4.times do
        post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key),
          params: +"Still cooling",
          headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
        assert_response :too_many_requests
        assert_equal "1", response.headers["Retry-After"]
      end

      # After 30s total, cooldown expires and posting works again
      travel 1.second
      post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key),
        params: +"Back online",
        headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
      assert_response :created
      assert_not @bot.reload.suspended?
    end
  end

  test "flood limit applies across rooms and attachments, ignores 422/404 requests, and isolates different bots" do
    @closed_room.memberships.grant_to(@bot)
    other_bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Other Bot", creator: users(:kevin), add_to_all_open_rooms: true)

    travel_to Time.zone.parse("2026-11-20 12:00:00 UTC") do
      # Blank (422) and nonexistent room (404) do not count towards the 10-message limit
      3.times do
        post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key), params: +"   ", headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
        assert_response :unprocessable_content
      end
      3.times do
        post room_bot_messages_url(999_999, @bot.bot_key), params: +"Missing", headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
        assert_response :not_found
      end

      # 5 in open room + 4 in closed room + 1 attachment = 10 messages
      5.times do |i|
        post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key), params: +"Open \#{i}", headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
        assert_response :created

**Integration Test Design for Bot Webhooks**

Okay, here's the plan. I need to comprehensively test the webhook integration, particularly how the bot handles various failure scenarios and edge cases. I'm going to focus my tests in `test/integration/bot_webhooks_test.rb`.

First, I need to nail down the *flooding flow*. This is the critical case where the bot is overwhelmed by a barrage of API posts combined with webhook mentions. I'll simulate this by firing API posts and triggering webhook replies simultaneously. I need to make sure the cooldown mechanism works as expected: that the webhook replies are suppressed, the API returns a `429` with a `Retry-After` header, and that retries during the cooldown are managed correctly, leading to bot suspension after five attempts. Importantly, I want to verify that a suspended bot returns `403` errors, ignores all webhook deliveries (mentions, room joins, even with `grant_all` in open rooms and direct mentions) and correctly remains listed as "Suspended" with the flooding reason. The test must conclude with an admin reactivation and a resumption of both API posts and webhook deliveries.

Next, I'll tackle the *failing webhook flow*. This scenario is just as important. I need to simulate 10 consecutive webhook failures. I will verify that the bot suspends after the 10th failure, and importantly, that all subsequent jobs (after the 10th failure) make *zero* HTTP requests. I need to confirm that new mentions and room joins (even queued) result in no jobs being enqueued and that the API continues to return `403` errors. The bot should correctly stay listed as "Suspended" with the "failing webhooks" reason. The test will need to cover the case of the owner fixing the webhook URL (the bot should remain suspended) and finally the administrator reactivation, with resumption of webhook deliveries and replies.

Finally, a crucial aspect is the handling of events when the bot is suspended. I need to explicitly verify that the creation of `Rooms::Open` and the `Membership.grant_all` action *do not* enqueue any webhooks for suspended bots, even when the `add_to_all_open_rooms: true` configuration is enabled.

I'm confident that with these integration tests in place, I will have a robust and well-tested webhook integration that handles failures and flooding gracefully. I'll get to it!

Here's my thinking on this issue:

**The Debugging Revelation: Timestamps, Ordering, and SQLite's Quirks**

Okay, I've got it! That *test_full_flooding_lifecycle...* test was failing because it was expecting "@Chatty Bot hello?" as the last message in `@room.messages.ordered`. The problem is within the `travel_to` block. It seems `Time.current` was frozen at precisely `12:00:10 UTC`. Consequently, *every single* message created during that moment ended up with the *exact* same `created_at` timestamp. And because the `Message.ordered` scope in this situation simply orders by `created_at` with no tie-breaker (like the `id`), SQLite, being SQLite, was returning these messages in an *arbitrary* order. This is a classic concurrency problem.

The correct way to check this scenario would be using `bot.messages.order(:id).last.plain_text_body` or `@room.messages.order(:id).last.plain_text_body` which looks at the actual *last* created message, regardless of timestamp. That's the key.

So, I need to adjust that assertion in `test/integration/bot_webhooks_test.rb` to reflect the correct way of retrieving the last message. Time to get that test passing and re-run the suite!

messages.content: Let's update `docs/bots.md` with design notes on automatic bot suspension, flooding protection, failing webhook tracking, and admin reactivation.
messages.thinking:
Okay, here's my take on those thoughts, tailored for an expert audience:

**Adding a Critical Section to the Bots Documentation**

Right, I need to make a key addition to the `docs/bots.md` document. I'm thinking a new section, and it should be concise and crystal clear. The title? Something straightforward like `### Automatic suspension (flooding and failing webhooks)`. It's crucial to cover this specific scenario, the automatic suspension triggered by excessive webhook failures or a rapid flood of requests, in our bot documentation. We need to be upfront about this common pitfall. The current docs might not make this connection readily. Time to improve them.

arguments.command:
cat <<'EOF' >> docs/bots.md

### Automatic suspension (flooding and failing webhooks)

- Suspended bots keep `status: :active` and are marked via `users.suspended_at` (`datetime`) and `users.suspension_reason` (`string`: `"flooding"` or `"failing_webhooks"`). Keeping `status: :active` preserves room memberships (including when editing closed rooms), historical messages, visibility on `/bots`, and counting toward the owner's `bots_per_member` limit without special-casing `User.active` across the app.
- Flooding protection (`User::Bot#consume_post_rate_limit!`, serialized via SQLite `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction):
  - Fixed limits in code (no settings): at most `10` messages in any sliding `10`-second window (`users.recent_post_timestamps` JSON array of UTC microsecond timestamps), `30`-second cooldown (`users.flood_cooldown_until`), and `5` attempts during the same cooldown (`users.flood_cooldown_attempts`) to suspend.
  - Shared by both API posts (`Messages::ByBotsController#create`, after validating non-blank payload) and webhook replies (`Webhook#handle_response`, after validating `200` + allowed content type + non-blank body).
  - The message exceeding 10 in 10s is rejected and starts a 30-second cooldown (`429 Too Many Requests` + `Retry-After` seconds left on API; webhook reply suppressed).
  - Five more post attempts during the same cooldown suspend the bot with reason `"flooding"` (API responds `403 Forbidden`; webhook reply suppressed). Waiting out the cooldown without hitting 5 attempts resets cooldown state cleanly.
- Failing webhook protection (`Webhook#record_delivery_failure!` / `#record_delivery_success!`, serialized via SQLite `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction):
  - `webhooks.consecutive_failures` tracks consecutive failed deliveries (any non-`2xx` HTTP response, timeout, or connection/network error) across both `mention` and `joined` events.
  - Any `2xx` (`Net::HTTPSuccess`) delivery resets `consecutive_failures` to `0`. Changing `webhook.url` also resets `consecutive_failures` without reactivating a suspended bot.
  - `10` failed deliveries in a row suspend the bot with reason `"failing_webhooks"`.
- Suspended bot behavior:
  - Posting API (`Messages::ByBotsController`) checks `ensure_not_suspended` right after `authenticate_bot` and responds `403 Forbidden`.
  - Webhooks are blocked both at enqueue time (`User.not_suspended` in `Message::Mentionee` and `Membership`) and at delivery time (`Webhook#deliverable_bot?` reloads `user` and skips suspended bots so queued jobs make no HTTP requests).
  - Listed on `/bots` (`app/views/bots/_bot.html.erb`) for both creator and administrators showing `"Suspended"` and the reason description.
- Reactivation:
  - `POST /bots/:bot_id/reactivation` (`Bots::ReactivationsController#create`), gated by `ensure_can_administer` (administrators only; members receive `403 Forbidden`).
  - Only administrators see the `"Reactivate"` button on `/bots`, with `data: { turbo_confirm: ... }` (native browser `confirm()` dialog).
  - `User::Bot#reactivate!` clears `suspended_at`, `suspension_reason`, cooldown/recent post timestamps, and `webhook.consecutive_failures` so the bot starts fresh immediately.
EOF
